_comment: Add a project = one entry. `detail` powers the click-through panel; omit it and the card just won't open.

projects.name: Cloe
projects.what: A local AI companion with persistent graph memory, an autonomous mind, four specialised sub-minds, and a transparent desktop presence.
does: Graph memory of roughly 6,700 nodes and 63,000 connections across five typed trees, and still growing
Confidence scoring with temporal decay, and a self-pruning compressor that protects core identity nodes
Four sub-minds she can hand work to: diagnostics, files and scheduling, 3D generation, image generation
A per-pixel-transparent Tauri v2 orb that stays click-through where it is transparent
Researches on its own while idle — mood-driven behaviour that does not wait to be spoken to

detail.intro: Cloe is not a chat window with a personality prompt on top. She is a stack: a Flask backend, local models, a memory that is a graph rather than a transcript, four sub-minds that each do one job, and a desktop orb with real per-pixel transparency. Everything runs on one consumer GPU. Nothing is sent anywhere.

sections.h: Memory is a graph, and it forgets on purpose
sections.p: Roughly 6,700 nodes and 63,000 connections across five typed trees — knowledge, mood, personality, relationship, desire — and the count climbs every day she is running, so treat that as a reading rather than a final size. Every node carries a confidence score that decays over time, so something reinforced once in April does not carry the same weight as something reinforced weekly.
bullets: Five typed trees rather than one flat store
Confidence scoring with temporal decay
A compressor scores nodes on several factors and prunes with Jaccard similarity matching
Core identity nodes are protected from pruning — she cannot compress away who she is

sections.h: Four sub-minds, and each one is its own service
sections.p: Work she cannot do in a language model gets handed to a separate program with its own lifecycle, its own UI panel and its own claim on the GPU. They are separate processes on purpose: a 3D forge running out of VRAM should take down the forge, not the assistant, and the card has to be handed between them cleanly rather than fought over.
bullets: Raphael — diagnostic watcher. Its own service on :5002, reading her logs live so a fault gets named rather than noticed three days later
Vretil — working assistant: files and scheduling in plain language, behind a book-shaped panel
Metatron — 3D prop forge, reference image or text to a textured GLB
Jophiel — image engine. FLUX.1 [schnell] to make a picture, Qwen-Image-Edit to change one, on a self-hosted ComfyUI

sections.h: Local models, and one of them is currently offline
sections.p: Mistral-Nemo 12B for conversation and qwen2.5-coder for a separate coding workspace, both hosted by a local Ollama instance and coordinated through one Flask backend. A third model, moondream, does vision — an image is described by it first, then reacted to in character by the conversational one, so what is in the picture and what she thinks about it stay separate jobs. That one is disconnected at the moment after a GPU swap and is waiting to be wired back in. It is listed here because it is part of the design, not because it is running today.

sections.h: The orb is genuinely transparent
sections.p: Built with Tauri v2, using per-pixel transparency and coordinate mapping so clicks pass through the transparent regions to whatever is behind. She sits on the desktop rather than in a window.

sections.h: She acts when nobody is talking to her
sections.p: Self-directed research during idle periods, mood-driven responses that are not replies to anything, a diary on a schedule, and a wake-word listener. There is also a Minecraft mod bridge that lets her participate in a game and make her own decisions in it.
bullets: Idle research loop
Autonomous mood-driven behaviour
Minecraft mod bridge with independent decision-making

sections.h: The failures are written up, not buried
sections.p: Several of the harder problems have their own write-ups in the repository — the VRAM co-residency crash that killed the forge and the crash-forensics tooling that came out of it, an engine-lifecycle port that caught a bug on the way through, a sandbox write-escape, and a lost-update race in the memory store with the stress-test numbers that proved it was real. Plain prose, no source dumps. Read them on GitHub.

shots.cap: The Skills panel — all four sub-minds live, each with its own sigil. The dormant sockets stay visibly empty rather than being hidden.
Her own stats view: memory reactor, current mood, system pulse, and the five mind trees with live node counts.

projects.name: Raphael
projects.what: The first sub-mind: a separate service that reads Cloe's own logs and says when something is wrong.
does: Runs as its own Flask service on :5002, independent of the assistant
Tails the logs live and matches them against a watchlist of patterns
Surfaces findings instead of burying them in a file nobody opens
Watchlist, sources and live feed kept apart — what to look for, where, and what is arriving

detail.intro: A system that writes logs nobody reads does not have diagnostics, it has an archive. Raphael is the thing that actually reads them: a separate process watching Cloe from the outside, matching what goes past against patterns worth caring about, and putting whatever it finds somewhere visible.

sections.h: Watching from outside is the point
sections.p: Raphael is a separate service, not a module. A watcher that lives inside the thing it watches goes down with it — and the moment you most want diagnostics is the moment the main process has stopped answering. Running apart means a fault gets named while it is happening rather than reconstructed three days later.

sections.h: Four panes, because they are four different questions
sections.p: The panel splits what a diagnostic tool actually has to answer, instead of pouring everything into one scrolling column.
bullets: Watchlist — the patterns being matched, and how many are active
Sources — which logs are being tailed right now
Live feed — what is streaming past this second
Findings — what actually matched, with counts, and an honest “no patterns matched yet” when nothing has

projects.name: Vretil
projects.what: Files and scheduling in plain language: find it, read it, write it, file it, remind me about it.
does: Browse, search, read, summarise, write and organise files by asking
Reminders that are one-off, recurring or weekday-scoped — and survive a restart
A cheap intent gate runs before the model, so ordinary chat pays nothing for the feature
Files land in flat top-level categories; new categories never nest
Sensitive application code needs explicit per-request confirmation

detail.intro: Vretil is the sub-mind that does the boring things: finding a file, writing one, putting it somewhere sensible, and remembering to mention it on Thursday. It runs through the conversational model that is already loaded rather than bringing its own, which on a single-GPU machine is the difference between a feature and a model swap.

sections.h: Flat beats tidy
sections.p: New files are classified against a registry of existing categories, and anything genuinely new gets a folder at the top level — never nested. Deep hierarchies look organised for about a month and then nobody can find anything. Flat and searchable survives contact with actual use.

sections.h: The gate is what makes it free
sections.p: A lightweight intent check runs before anything reaches a model, so a normal conversation never pays for the filesystem feature. Only a request that actually looks like one goes further — and when it does, new content is resolved against what already exists, appending to a log or overwriting a correction as the case warrants, rather than dropping a near-duplicate beside it.

sections.h: Two one-line bugs worth the mention
sections.p: Both surfaced only on real hardware and both were a single line. The panel was missing from the clickable list during an orb collapse, so it stopped taking clicks at exactly the wrong moment; and the resize handles sat outside the registered click-through region, so they looked draggable and were not. Neither shows up in code review. They show up when somebody actually clicks the thing. Write-up on GitHub.

facts: Book panel — chat left, contents right

projects.name: Metatron
projects.what: A local image-to-3D forge. Feed it one reference photo, get back a textured mesh.
does: Runs Hunyuan3D locally on a single consumer GPU
Schedules its own VRAM so a 12GB card can host the forge and a language model without either dying
Job queue, live forge log, in-browser preview of the result
Polygon budget honoured end to end — ask for 100k faces and you get 100k
Four status lights are real probes against the running process, not assumed state

detail.intro: Image-to-3D generation usually means uploading your reference to somebody else's GPU and waiting. Metatron runs the whole pipeline on one machine — background removal, generation, texture painting — and gives it a control room: a queue you can watch, a log that says what stage it is at, and a viewer to orbit the result before you keep it.

sections.h: The hard part was memory, not modelling
sections.p: A 12GB card cannot hold a 3D diffusion engine (~8.5GB resident) and a language model (~7–8GB) at once. The ordering turned out to be the whole bug: VRAM has to be clear *before* the engine starts loading, not while. Getting that wrong meant twelve-minute warm-ups with both models resident and the machine frozen solid — no crash, no log, nothing to read afterwards. A keepalive thread quietly reloading the 7GB brain every 60 seconds made it worse. Threads now check ownership of the card before re-warming, and a 535-sample flight-recorder run held the language model at zero VRAM for 18 unbroken minutes through a full engine boot and forge cycle — against about 50 seconds before the fix.

sections.h: Built to be watched
sections.p: Every forge reports elapsed time and current stage — removing background, generating, texturing — so a seven-minute job is legible rather than a spinner. Failures name what died and when.
bullets: Queue with retry and discard per job
Per-job elapsed time and stage
In-browser mesh preview before approval
Output straight to GLB, ready for Blender

sections.h: Freezes leave no evidence, so I built some
sections.p: A hard freeze writes almost nothing to the Windows event log, which makes it the worst kind of bug: it costs an hour and tells you nothing. So Metatron grew its own forensics — a flight recorder that samples lazily when idle and every two seconds under load, a session seal that can tell a process that died from one that was killed, and a root-cause ranker that reports its own confidence, from hardware-confirmed down to no-data. The write-up is on GitHub.

projects.name: Jophiel
projects.what: Local image generation and editing, on the same 12GB card everything else is already fighting over.
does: Text to image with FLUX.1 [schnell] on a self-hosted ComfyUI — no API, no per-image cost
Text-instructed editing of an existing image with Qwen-Image-Edit
Quantised GGUF build chosen to fit the VRAM budget beside the rest of Cloe
Explicit engine on/off rather than a resident model holding the card hostage
Two modes that look different on purpose, so you always know which one you are in

detail.intro: Jophiel is the fourth sub-mind and the second heavy engine, which is what made it the awkward one to add: the card was already spoken for. Generation and editing are one skill in two modes — Quill makes a picture, Eye changes one — and an image can be thrown from either to the other.

sections.h: Two modes, told apart by how they move
sections.p: Both modes share a layout — showcase image, filmstrip history, prompt bar — so the only thing separating them could have been a word in the header. Instead they have different visual languages: soft ink-bloom motion for generation, a slowly rotating iris and scan-line for editing. You know which mode you are in before you have read anything.

sections.h: The engine that would not die
sections.p: The first build stopped the wrapper process and reported the engine off. It was not off — the real engine was still resident and still holding VRAM, which on a shared 12GB card is the whole problem wearing a disguise. The fix was Metatron's: kill the process tree, not the parent. Verified by actually restarting and watching the memory come back, because the bug's entire nature was reporting success while failing. Write-up on GitHub.

facts: Generation live end to end; edit mode in progress

projects.name: Mytheder
projects.what: A Czech party card game, rebuilt from an abandoned repo and given a new identity for a Discord community.
does: Private rooms, five-character join codes, no accounts
1016 cards across five themed packs, loaded from JSON — no database
Chat, reconnect with backoff, rooms held open 90 seconds for dropped players
Whole theme is three colour tokens: re-skinning is a config change

detail.intro: The original author shut the project down and released the code. I rebuilt it: deleted the database, removed the dead accounts system, wrote the chat that was never finished, and re-skinned it for a Discord server that wanted its own version. It now runs as part of this site rather than on somebody's spare subdomain.

sections.h: The database was doing nothing
sections.p: The game only ever read cards from MySQL — three queries, no writes. All 1016 cards now load from JSON at boot and the entire database layer is gone. Adding cards is editing a file; there are no migrations.

sections.h: Most of the work was failure handling
sections.p: The bugs that actually ruined games were never about rules.
bullets: A one-second auth timeout was fine on localhost and killed every real connection through a proxy
One dropped socket ended everyone's game, because rooms were destroyed the moment they fell below three players
A small pack could run its prompt pile dry and take the room down with it
A player who dropped out of a full game was locked out by a headcount they were still part of

sections.h: Re-skinnable by design
sections.p: The first build hard-coded one accent colour across ten components. Every colour now resolves from three tokens, so giving a new community its own version is a config change and four images rather than a hunt through the codebase.

projects.name: Monkey Paw
projects.what: One player makes a wish. Everyone else writes the catch that makes them regret it.
does: Free text instead of a deck — nothing ever runs out
A monkey's paw curls one finger per wish spent
Czech or English, chosen per room
Built on everything the card game taught me

detail.intro: A party game with no cards. The chooser writes a wish; everyone else writes the twist that ruins it; the chooser picks the one that hurt most. Because the content is typed rather than dealt, it never repeats and never runs out.

sections.h: Free text changes the failure modes
sections.p: A card game can always play a random card for someone who has gone quiet. You cannot autogenerate a person's joke — so a timed-out player gets a funny stock line instead of an empty slot, and three consecutive misses flips their paw over until they come back.

sections.h: The paw is the clock, then it isn't
sections.p: Each player's paw closes a finger per wish they spend. Round count is fixed when the game starts, so somebody who wanders off ends with fingers still up — a visible record of having been away — rather than holding the game open forever.
